hints: Notice the two sources start in phase, so the $90^{\circ}$ phase difference at X must come only from the extra distance one wave travels.
Recall that a path difference of one full wavelength $\lambda$ corresponds to a phase change of $360^{\circ}$.
Set up the fraction $\frac{\text{path difference}}{\lambda} \times 360^{\circ} = 90^{\circ}$ and solve for the path difference.
walkthrough: The sources oscillate in phase, so any phase difference at point X is caused by the difference in distances travelled, called the path difference $\Delta x$.
For waves of wavelength $\lambda$, the rule is phase difference $= \frac{\Delta x}{\lambda} \times 360^{\circ}$.
Here the required phase difference is $90^{\circ}$, so $\frac{\Delta x}{\lambda} \times 360^{\circ} = 90^{\circ}$.
Adding a whole number of wavelengths would give the same $90^{\circ}$ effect, but $\frac{\lambda}{4}$ is the smallest possible value and matches one of the options. This is option B.

options.A: A path difference of $\frac{\lambda}{8}$ gives a phase difference of only $45^{\circ}$, not $90^{\circ}$.
options.B: A path difference of $\frac{\lambda}{4}$ gives a phase difference of $90^{\circ}$ because one full wavelength equals $360^{\circ}$.
options.C: A path difference of $\frac{\lambda}{2}$ gives a phase difference of $180^{\circ}$, which is antiphase, not $90^{\circ}$.
options.D: A path difference of $\lambda$ gives a phase difference of $360^{\circ}$, which is equivalent to $0^{\circ}$ or in phase.
